title: Chiral near-fields at achiral plasmonic tips enable nanoscale valley polarimetry
authors: Jonggeun Hwang, Kijeong Park, Hyeongwoo Lee, Yeonjeong Koo, SeokJae Yoo, Long Ju, Kyoung-Duck Park
abstract: Optical helicity is central to chiral light-matter interactions, yet plasmonic confinement typically distorts it at the nanoscale. Here, we demonstrate nanoscale valley polarimetry using an achiral Au tip, where incidence-angle control of circularly polarized light creates a strongly localized, helicity-preserving near-field. Chiral tip-enhanced photoluminescence (c-TEPL) directly resolves and reverses local valley polarization in monolayer WSe2 and reveals nanoscale polarization variations in strained MoS2 hidden by diffraction-limited measurements.
summary: The paper introduces chiral tip-enhanced photoluminescence (c-TEPL) as a novel technique to measure valley polarization in 2D semiconductors. By controlling the angle of circularly polarized light incident on an achiral plasmonic tip, the researchers generate a localized, helicity-preserving near-field. This allows for nanoscale mapping of valley polarization, revealing strain-induced effects previously hidden by conventional, diffraction-limited measurements.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving nanoscale valley polarimetry to locally resolve the degree and sign of valley polarization in atomically thin semiconductors, overcoming the limitations of diffraction-limited measurements.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that using chiral near-fields generated at achiral plasmonic tips enables valley polarimetry, successfully revealing nanoscale variations in valley polarization in strained MoS2.
method: The core technique is Chiral Tip-Enhanced Photoluminescence (c-TEPL), which measures the difference in photoluminescence intensity when exciting with $\sigma^+$ versus $\sigma^-$ circularly polarized light.
model_or_system: The study uses monolayer Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDs) like WSe2 and MoS2, coupled with an achiral Au tip. The mechanism relies on controlling the incidence angle of circularly polarized light to generate a helicity-preserving near-field.
key_observables: Degree of Valley Polarization (DOP, $ho$), PL spectra under $\sigma^+$ vs. $\sigma^-$ excitation, and spatial maps of the near-field Stokes parameters ($S_{0,\parallel}, S_{3,\parallel}$).
important_parameters: Incidence angle ($	heta_{inc} = 35^\circ$ is optimal), tip-sample separation ($\le 10$ nm), and the material's strain state.
main_assumptions: The technique assumes that controlling the incidence angle of CPL light on an achiral tip is sufficient to generate the necessary chiral near-field for valley resolution.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the c-TEPL setup, show the dependence of DOP on excitation polarization (CPL vs. LPL), and map the spatial distribution of DOP across a nanogap, comparing near-field results to far-field measurements.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the necessity of the technique by showing the angle dependence of the near-field polarization. It then applies this technique to map valley polarization in WSe2, confirming helicity dependence. Finally, it applies the method to MoS2 to map strain-induced valley polarization variations across a nanogap.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, non-destructive optical tool to probe fundamental quantum properties (valley polarization) at the nanoscale, which is crucial for designing next-generation 2D electronic and photonic devices.
